claims.text: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles contain at least five principal elements.
Rapid heating and cooling limit atomic mobility in the nanoparticles.
Limited atomic mobility promotes a random or highly mixed elemental distribution.
Limited atomic mobility kinetically traps a single-phase solid solution.
Increasing the high-temperature dwell time while holding heating and cooling rates fixed increases atomic diffusion.
Unfavorable mixing enthalpies can favor elemental segregation or alternative structures when atomic mobility is sufficient.
Atomic-size mismatch promotes segregation and nucleation of secondary phases in the targeted nanoparticles.
A mixed precursor containing more than five noble-metal salts can be reduced to form HEA nanoparticles.
Increasing the number of constituent elements intrinsically favors a more random nanoparticle.
The relevant rapid-processing regime can involve heating to about 2000 K within milliseconds and cooling faster than 10^4 K/s.
Keeping the extended process short prevents particle growth.
Ultrafast cycling leaves insufficient time for atoms to approach thermodynamic equilibrium.
Stochastic reduction of mixed precursors under limited mobility produces a homogeneous, metastable single phase.
A roughly 55 ms thermal-shock baseline with cooling faster than 10^4 K/s exhibits single-phase solid-solution behavior.
Moderately increasing dwell time will increase elemental segregation, compositional gradients, or secondary-phase formation relative to the baseline.
XRD peak splitting or additional peaks would indicate formation of secondary phases.
Heterogeneous STEM-EDS elemental maps would indicate elemental segregation.
The mechanism may not apply to solution-based or prolonged high-temperature processing because equilibrium phase separation is already expected there.
The dwell-time threshold for segregation depends on the elemental combination, precursor configuration, heating power, and substrate interactions.
Failure of one prolonged-dwell sample to show increased segregation relative to the baseline would refute the limited-mobility hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis states that the segregation threshold is unknown and composition-dependent, but treats a negative result at one unspecified extended dwell as decisive refutation. That dwell may simply remain below the relevant mobility threshold.
